title: Evaluating Movements of Co‐Occurring Silver and Bighead Carp in a Small Missouri River Tributary
content:
ABSTRACT

Silver Carp Hypophthalmichthys molitrix and Bighead Carp Hypophthalmichthys nobilis commonly inhabit small tributaries of mainstem rivers. However, dynamic environmental conditions within these systems may influence their movement patterns differently than in larger rivers, potentially leading to important implications regarding their range expansion. We investigated the effects of various environmental (water temperature and discharge), biological (species and sex), temporal (season and year), and spatial (tagging region) variables on Silver and Bighead Carp movements in the Little Sioux River, a small tributary of the Missouri River in northwest Iowa from 2022 to 2024 using passive acoustic telemetry. We used generalized linear mixed models to evaluate (1) the probability individuals moved on a weekly basis and (2) the magnitude (distance; rkm) of their movement events. We assessed maximum ranges and compared them between species, sexes, and among tagging locations. Movement probability was highest and movement events were typically largest during high discharge events (> 30 m3/s) and warmer water temperatures (> 15°C) during spring and early summer. Silver Carp movement probability was higher than Bighead Carp during these conditions, with up to 63% of individuals moving during a given week, as opposed to 36% for Bighead Carp. Both upstream and downstream movements were observed during spring and summer, but the frequency of movement types each season was variable across years. During fall, movements were infrequent and primarily downstream. Total ranges were highest for individuals tagged in the lower region and lowest for fish in the middle tagging region. Our results suggest Silver and Bighead Carp movement in small rivers is driven by similar environmental factors as in larger systems, but dynamic environmental conditions could potentially cause high interannual variation in movement.
